drills.q: What are the two ways of finding out where a program spends time?
options: Instrumenting, which inserts code at every entry and exit, and sampling, which interrupts and records
Timing the whole program, and timing each function
Reading hardware counters, and reading the system clock
Static analysis, and tracing
drills.why: They are biased in opposite directions, which is why knowing which one a tool is doing matters more than knowing its name.

options: Small functions called very often, because the overhead follows call count rather than time
Large functions, because they take longer to enter and leave
Functions that allocate memory
Recursive functions, because each level is counted twice
drills.why: A tiny function called a billion times is measured mostly measuring the measurement.

drills.q: Why is a profiled instrumented binary not the binary you ship?
options: Instrumentation inhibits inlining, so functions exist that would have disappeared at -O2
It is built without optimisation
The profiler rewrites the machine code as it runs
Debug information changes the layout of the code
drills.why: The function you spent an afternoon staring at may not exist in the shipped build at all.

options: Something rare and expensive, because it will not be interrupted while it happens
Something hot, because samples merge into the surrounding frames
Time spent in the standard library
Anything in a function that was inlined
drills.why: An event of a hundred microseconds that happens once will be missed at any sane rate, whatever it did to the person who hit it.

drills.q: Why is the recorded address not the guilty instruction?
options: The interrupt arrives some cycles after the event that caused it
The profiler records the return address rather than the current one
Optimisation reorders instructions after the profile is taken
The address is rounded to a cache line
drills.why: Attribution at instruction granularity is fiction unless the hardware's precise sampling mode is switched on.

drills.q: Why do profilers sample at 999 hertz rather than 1000?
options: A round rate aliases against everything else in the system that runs at a round rate
999 is the highest rate the kernel permits
It leaves one sample per second for bookkeeping
It reduces overhead by a measurable amount
drills.why: A prime offset from every round number means the sampler does not keep landing at the same point in someone else's cycle.

drills.q: Your program is slow because it waits on a lock. What does a processor sampling profile show?
options: An almost idle machine, and nothing about the waiting
The lock function, at the top of the profile
The thread holding the lock
A warning that most samples were unattributable
drills.why: This is the most common way a profile misleads. The fix is to sample the scheduler switching threads out rather than the processor.

drills.q: What does a frame pointer walk need to work?
options: Every frame in the stack to have kept its frame pointer
Debug information for every function on the stack
The program to be compiled without optimisation
The stack to fit inside one page
drills.why: Miss one and the walk either stops or follows garbage, so a single library built without them truncates every stack that passes through it.

drills.q: What does unwinding through the compiler's exception tables cost, compared to a frame pointer walk?
options: Kilobytes of copied stack per sample, dropped samples at high rates, silent truncation, and slow reporting
Nothing; it is strictly better and needs no rebuild
It requires the program to be single threaded
It only works on optimised builds
drills.why: It does work without a rebuild, which is its real advantage. The costs are what sent the industry back to frame pointers.

drills.q: Roughly what does compiling with frame pointers cost?
options: Around a percent typically, with a few percent on some builds and nothing measurable on many servers
Around twenty percent, which is why they were removed
Nothing at all under any circumstances
It depends entirely on the number of function calls, and is usually over ten percent
drills.why: Two major distributions turned them back on in 2023 and 2024, having decided that a profile you can read is worth a percent.

drills.q: In a flame graph, what does the width of a box mean?
options: The fraction of samples that contained that frame
How long that call took, on the time axis
How many times the function was called
How much memory the function allocated
drills.why: It is not a timeline, and left to right order carries no meaning beyond sorting. A flame chart, where the x axis is time, is a different thing.

drills.q: Which flame graph answers the question you usually have?
options: The differential one, coloured by what grew and shrank between two profiles
The plain one, where you look at the widest tower
The off processor one, always
The memory one, weighted by bytes
drills.why: The widest tower is usually something you already knew about. What changed is the question you actually had.

drills.q: A load generator sends a request every ten milliseconds. The system stalls for one second. What does a naive tool record?
options: One slow sample, because it sent nothing while it was waiting
A hundred slow samples, one per interval
Nothing, because the requests timed out
A hundred samples of ten milliseconds each
drills.why: The requests that would have been slow were never sent. The tool coordinated with the system under test and stopped asking while it struggled.

options: Measure latency from when a request was due to be sent, not from when it was actually sent
Increase the number of load generator threads
Discard the slowest one percent of samples as outliers
Sample at a prime frequency
drills.why: That single change turns one slow sample into the many slow samples the world would have experienced, and makes the percentile honest.

drills.q: A benchmark library's function to keep a result alive. What does it not do?
options: Stop the compiler from simplifying or folding the expression that produced the result
Prevent the result from being discarded
Work at any optimisation level
Apply to values in registers
drills.why: What you are keeping alive is the answer, not the work. A constant folded computation is still constant folded, and the timing then measures nothing.
